<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-grounded cases and executed the Pressure Questions/Answer format correctly. The decisive asymmetry is that A's core diagnosis—platform self-dealing (the same company profiting from both primary sale and markup) creates a structural incentive against self-correction—was never squarely refuted by B, only answered with a different proposed remedy (separate ticketing from resale, ban bots), which concedes the diagnosis while dodging why the specific cap is worse than the status quo on that dimension. A also handled the enforcement-comparison pressure question cleanly by distinguishing real-time bot detection from after-the-fact ledger auditing, giving the cap a plausible mechanism B's "same failure mode" reply didn't fully dislodge. B's strongest counter—that leakage concentrates precisely in the highest-stakes, most fraud-prone tickets—was a sharp, under-addressed point in A's closing, but it operates as a severity-weighted objection to an already-narrowed "outlier" category, whereas A's unanswered self-dealing point strikes at the core justification for regulation itself. A's closing ("guaranteed harm vs. contingent harm") also gave a cleaner overall decision rule than B's narrower "protect where stakes are highest" frame. The debate was close and well-fought, but A's throughline was slightly more complete.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's [A1.4]/[A4.4] platform self-dealing charge, which B only answered by proposing a different remedy rather than refuting the underlying incentive problem, versus B's [B4.4] "trickle is exactly the high-stakes tickets" reframe, which A never fully neutralized but which addressed a narrower slice of the case.</best_rebuttal>
